newsitem.title: USA: Music trade fair will not invite Cubans to Miami.
newsitem.headline: Music trade fair will not invite Cubans to Miami.

text.p: A major music industry trade fair aimed at promoting Latin American music has bowed to political pressure and will feature no Cuban performers when it takes place in Miami in September.

More than 20 acts ranging from reggae to salsa are lined up to play during the four-day MIDEM Latin American and Caribbean Music Market, a gathering of artists, agents, publishers and other industry figures.
But organisers said they had decided against inviting any perfomers from the Communist-ruled island to avoid friction with sectors of Miami's Cuban exile community.

"Although we know Cuba is one of the most prolific countries in terms of talent at the moment, we don't want to hurt the feelings of part of the Cuban community here," MIDEM artistic director Bernard Batzen told the Fort Lauderdale Sun-Sentinel.
"It's a political problem and it's too bad that art and politics are mixed. But we are not here to change the world or relations between Cuba and the U.S. It's a shame we can't, but it's a fact."
Batzen confirmed to Reuters there would be no Cuban acts but declined to discuss the issue further.

Cuban exiles in Miami have a history of hounding artists they deem sympathetic to President Fidel Castro's government. One Spanish-language radio station, Tropical 98.3 FM, broke new ground in March by playing music by Cuban pop stars, but it was forced to stop after advertisers cancelled spots and a bomb threat was phoned in.
Cuban-U.S. cultural exchanges are permitted despite a U.S. embargo on the island and Cuban musical groups such as Los Van Van have performed to acclaim elsewhere in the United States.

Judy Cantor, an expert on Cuban music who writes for Miami's New Times weekly, said she was disappointed by MIDEM's position. "There's definitely an explosion in Cuban music, and evryone is appreciating it except in Miami," she said. "There is an audience for it here. A minority is spoiling it for everyone else."

MIDEN chief executive Xavier Roy, asked about a possible ban on Cuban performers at a news conference last September, said he believed music should not be a political issue. But he did not specify if MIDEM intended to invite Cubans.

French-based MIDEM (International Record, Music Publishing and Video Music Market) also holds annual fairs in Cannes and Hong Kong. The Sept. 8-11 Miami event will be its first dedicated to Latin and Caribbean music.
